title: Large UK Biobank study links early depression symptoms to higher Parkinson's risk
summary: A study of nearly 452,000 UK Biobank participants found that people with early depressive symptoms had a 36% higher risk of later developing Parkinson's disease. Fat-related metabolic changes may partly explain the link, and the association appeared stronger in people with existing genetic susceptibility. The findings point to depression as a possible early marker rather than a cause.

title: FDA clears Empatica wearable platform for continuous Parkinson's symptom monitoring
summary: The FDA granted 510(k) clearance to Empatica's Health Monitoring Platform for Parkinson's disease, which uses wrist-worn sensors, a patient app, and a clinician portal to track bradykinesia, dyskinesia, tremor, sleep quality, and medication compliance over time. It's the company's twelfth FDA clearance and builds on its 2025 acquisition of PKG Health's symptom-tracking algorithms.

title: Developer raises $36M to help fund Phase 3 trial of app-paired levodopa treatment
summary: Remepy raised $36 million in financing that will partly fund a Phase 3 trial of Hybridopa, which pairs standard levodopa medication with an AI-driven mobile app (DopApp) offering cognitive training and rehabilitation support. This account is based on a company funding announcement, not a peer-reviewed result, though it references an earlier published pilot study.

title: More physical activity linked to slower motor and cognitive decline in Parkinson's
summary: A longitudinal analysis using data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative found that people with higher physical activity levels showed slower decline in rigidity, axial motor symptoms, and cognitive measures. Notably, the protective association wasn't explained by better preservation of dopamine transporter levels, suggesting activity may help through other brain mechanisms beyond dopamine protection.

title: Why Parkinson's and Alzheimer's may be more biologically connected than once thought
summary: MJFF Chief Scientist Mark Frasier discusses growing evidence that Parkinson's and Alzheimer's overlap more than previously recognized, with an estimated 30-50% of Alzheimer's patients also showing Parkinson's-associated markers like alpha-synuclein alongside amyloid or tau. New biomarker tools now let researchers detect these overlapping pathologies in living patients, which could open the door to more personalized treatment approaches instead of treating the diseases as fully separate.

title: Phase II trial of GBA1-targeted drug pariceract discontinued after no benefit shown
summary: Bial's Phase II trial of BIA 28-6156 (pariceract), a precision-medicine drug targeting GBA1-related Parkinson's disease, found no safety concerns but also no difference in disease progression compared with the control group. The company has discontinued further development of the drug. It's a reminder that precision-medicine approaches don't automatically translate into clinical benefit, even when the underlying biological rationale is sound.

title: MJFF outlines 2026 federal and state policy priorities for Parkinson's
summary: The Michael J. Fox Foundation laid out its 2026 policy agenda, including a push for federal NIH Parkinson's research funding to reach $600 million annually by fiscal year 2028, continued state-level research investment, tighter restrictions on environmental toxins such as paraquat, and full implementation of the National Parkinson's Project. The Foundation is mobilizing its advocate network to press these priorities with policymakers.

title: Researchers map a brain-signal "cascade" behind Parkinson's motor symptoms
summary: In a study of 23 people with Parkinson's disease undergoing deep brain stimulation surgery, researchers recorded brain signals from the motor cortex and a deep brain structure called the globus pallidus. They found that bursts of a particular brain-wave pattern in the cortex trigger a cascade that amplifies related activity deeper in the brain, a pattern linked to worsened motor symptoms. Dopamine medication reduced this cascade and improved symptoms, offering a more detailed picture of how these signals contribute to Parkinson's motor problems.

title: Study finds diverging links between diabetes, metformin, and Parkinson's risk
summary: A genetic and epidemiological study examined whether type 2 diabetes and the diabetes drug metformin affect Parkinson's disease risk. Using Mendelian randomization alongside a national patient cohort and an FDA adverse-event database, the researchers found type 2 diabetes was linked to lower Parkinson's risk in one analysis, while metformin use was consistently associated with higher risk of parkinsonism. The authors describe this as opposing effects of diabetes and metformin on Parkinson's risk, and suggest clinicians watch for neurological symptoms in patients taking metformin.

title: Small study finds visual-feedback training may improve balance in Parkinson's
summary: In a small study of 21 people with early-to-moderate Parkinson's disease, researchers tested whether adding visual-feedback balance training to standard physical therapy improved mobility. After four weeks of combined treatment using a balance-training platform, participants showed improved balance, walking speed, and functional independence, with benefits still present six months later. Because the study didn't include a comparison group and enrolled few participants, the authors say larger controlled trials are needed before drawing firm conclusions.

title: Major Parkinson's organizations submit joint priorities for first National Plan to End Parkinson's
summary: The American Parkinson Disease Association, the Michael J. Fox Foundation, and the Parkinson's Foundation submitted joint recommendations to the NIH ahead of an Advisory Council meeting on the first National Plan to End Parkinson's. The recommendations outline six priorities to pursue by 2035, including reducing financial burden on patients and families, preventing disease and slowing progression, and researching environmental triggers such as the herbicide paraquat. The submission follows a public comment period that closed August 22, 2026.

title: Starting rehabilitation therapy early after Parkinson's diagnosis linked to longer survival
summary: A South Korean nationwide cohort study followed 19,153 people with Parkinson's disease for up to 15 years and compared survival based on when they began rehabilitation therapy after diagnosis. People who waited one to two years to start had a 28% higher risk of death, and those who waited two or more years had a 44% higher risk, compared with people who began within the first year. The association held regardless of disability severity at diagnosis. As an observational study, it shows a link rather than proof that early rehab itself extends life.

title: Blood markers of brain injury, combined with air pollution exposure, linked to Parkinson's and dementia risk
summary: A study of nearly 19,645 UK Biobank participants over age 50 examined two blood proteins that signal brain-cell damage, neurofilament light and GFAP, alongside air pollution exposure. Higher neurofilament light levels were associated with greater risk of later developing Parkinson's disease or dementia, or of dying during follow-up, and fine-particulate air pollution appeared to strengthen that link. GFAP was more specifically tied to dementia risk. The findings are associational, not proof that pollution or these proteins cause neurodegeneration, but suggest blood tests could eventually help flag people at higher risk.

title: Non-invasive nerve stimulation improves bladder test results in Parkinson's, but not always how patients feel
summary: A meta-analysis pooling seven studies and 591 people with Parkinson's disease examined non-invasive tibial nerve stimulation, a mild electrical pulse delivered near the ankle, as a treatment for urinary symptoms. The therapy measurably improved bladder capacity and control on lab measurements, but patients didn't consistently report less urgency, frequency, or nighttime urination. The mismatch suggests the treatment may help physiologically without necessarily being felt as symptom relief, and the authors call for further study of real-world outcomes.

title: Small study finds standard canes may slow walking speed in Parkinson's despite patient satisfaction
summary: In a secondary analysis of 50 people with Parkinson's disease, researchers compared walking with and without a standard cane. Cane use was associated with about 0.25 meters per second slower walking speed and smaller steps, a clinically meaningful decline, yet most participants reported no reduction in fear of falling and said they were satisfied with the cane. Because the study was small and not a full randomized trial, the authors say the mismatch between measured effect and patient experience is worth discussing with clinicians rather than treated as settled.

title: Diabetes drugs called GLP-1 agonists linked to lower dementia risk, weaker signal for Parkinson's
summary: A real-world study matched 46,962 people with obesity and type 2 diabetes to compare outcomes for those started on GLP-1 receptor agonists, a drug class that includes Ozempic-type medications, against other diabetes drugs. GLP-1 users had a lower rate of dementia (4.8% versus 7.8%). For Parkinson's disease specifically, the main comparison showed a similar downward trend that was not statistically significant, though a narrower comparison against one other drug class did find a significant reduction. The dementia-protective signal looks fairly solid; the Parkinson's-specific signal is suggestive but weaker and shouldn't be reported as confirmed.
